claims.text: Variations in local lattice distortion and chemical short-range order explain differences in deformation and failure among the quinary alloy and its subsets.
Local lattice distortions and chemical short-range order govern dislocation nucleation and mobility.
Chemical short-range order develops during thermomechanical processing of the compared alloys.
The controlled comparison will use single-phase FCC alloys with comparable grain sizes and dislocation densities.
Identical thermomechanical treatment can provide comparable initial microstructures across the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
The experiment compares equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys under identical processing histories using in situ mechanical testing and high-resolution characterization.
Local lattice strains and chemical short-range order will be measured using TEM, diffuse scattering, and atom-probe tomography.
Local lattice distortions and short-range chemical order act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has greater local lattice distortion than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy develops more pronounced short-range chemical order than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Greater distortion and ordering in the quinary alloy produce stronger dislocation pinning and higher barriers to dislocation nucleation.
Stronger dislocation pinning and higher nucleation barriers increase yield strength and sustain work hardening.
The quaternary and ternary alloys develop less local heterogeneity because they contain fewer constituent species.
Reduced local heterogeneity in the quaternary and ternary alloys causes weaker dislocation interactions and earlier strain localization.
The quinary alloy will have higher yield strength than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The quinary alloy will have a greater work-hardening rate than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Yield strength and work-hardening trends will correlate positively with measured lattice distortion and short-range-order parameters.
The proposed mechanism applies at controlled strain rates and room to moderately elevated temperatures where dislocation motion and local-ordering effects remain active.
Mn-related magnetic effects may also contribute to the mechanical-property differences.

The hypothesis is falsified if mechanical-property differences do not correlate with lattice distortion or short-range order, including if those features are similar despite differing mechanical performance.

contradictions.description: The framing seeks an explanation for which constituent count alone is inadequate, but the proposed mechanism assumes a monotonic constituent-count hierarchy—more species produce more distortion and ordering and therefore better properties—without specifying chemistry-dependent exceptions or demonstrating that count is not the operative variable.
